This proposal disables the ability to add new value to the Sapling chain value pool balance. From NU8 activation, every transaction’s Sapling value balance must be nonnegative: value may leave the
, or move between Sapling notes, but no new value may enter it. Coinbase transactions may no longer contain Sapling outputs.

The cost of doing so is low. Excluding mining pool coinbase shielding and the Zcash Community Grants funding stream, which can move to Ironwood (see Open issues), only 1.2% of non-coinbase transactions in the last 30 days touched the

As fewer transactions use the pool, individual Sapling transactions may become easier to distinguish by timing and amount, as is true of any shielded pool with low usage, but the unlinkability of spent notes from the transactions that created them is unaffected.
Full nodes change behaviour at the NU8 activation height, and from that height consensus prevents all wallets from adding value to the

, so wallets also change behaviour at that height in this respect. When a wallet chooses to migrate its users’ Sapling funds is not constrained to a single height; using a common migration procedure (ZIP 318
) limits how much that choice distinguishes wallets.
No new value can enter the
after activation, from any transaction version, including coinbase.
Holders keep full access to their Sapling funds. They can spend to any other pool (in practice Ironwood or transparent), and can keep making Sapling-to-Sapling transfers, including to other people.
No change to the Sapling circuits or parameters, and no new trusted setup.
The consensus change is small and easy to analyse.
This ZIP does not set a date after which Sapling notes can no longer be spent. That is left to a future proposal. So is what happens to any value left in the pool at that point.
This ZIP does not make Sapling quantum recoverable.

For a Sapling-source migration, each canonical migration transaction has exactly one Sapling spend in place of the single Orchard spend, with the Sapling bundle padded so that the presence or absence of a Sapling change output is not observable, and no spends from any other pool. Mixing source pools within one transaction or one migration schedule would link a user’s Sapling and Orchard holdings, so each migration is restricted to one source pool.
Requirements for wallets and node software
Wallets MUST NOT create transactions that contain one or more Sapling outputs together with one or more inputs from outside the
(transparent inputs, or spends from any other shielded pool). As with ZIP 211
, this is stricter than consensus, for usability reasons. Consensus would accept a mixed transaction whose Sapling spends cover its Sapling outputs.
Wallets SHOULD NOT create new Unified Addresses that include a Sapling receiver. They MAY keep producing Sapling receivers before activation for compatibility.
Wallets that hold Sapling funds SHOULD offer to migrate them to the
. Wallets SHOULD use the migration procedure of ZIP 318
Block template software SHOULD reject Sapling-only miner addresses with a clear error.
Transactions signed for an earlier consensus branch become invalid at NU8 activation under ZIP 200
, so no mempool-specific rule is needed.
Why a balance rule, not a circuit change

The rule mirrors ZIP 211 for Sprout and ZIP 2006 for Orchard. It only needs a check on a field validators already parse. It does not touch the Sapling Spend or Output circuits. That avoids a new parameter generation ceremony, any risk of a soundness regression in Groth16 circuits, and any new transaction version. The implementation is a few lines in each full validator, and its security is easy to analyse.
ZIP 2006 also disabled cross-address transfers within the
. That was possible because the new Orchard Action circuit had an
. Doing the same for Sapling would need a new Sapling circuit and trusted setup, which this ZIP sets out to avoid.
Allowing Sapling outputs also lets wallets keep using Sapling change when withdrawing, so a withdrawal reveals only the amount leaving the pool rather than the total value of the notes spent.
Why the coinbase prohibition is explicit
ZIP 213 has allowed coinbase outputs to Sapling addresses since Heartwood

, but miners have not adopted it: only one Mainnet block has ever paid its coinbase to a Sapling output. {TODO: cite the block height and txid.} Shielded coinbase has instead moved to the Orchard protocol, which since NU6.3 pays into the
. In the 30 days to height 3,532,124, 4.6% of blocks paid their coinbase directly to the
, and none contained a Sapling output.
Leaving Sapling coinbase outputs available invites zero-value or misconfigured outputs that add commitments with no purpose. The explicit rule matches the ZIP 2006 Orchard rule.
This ZIP is proposed for deployment in the NU8 network upgrade.

58.8% of all Sapling transactions in the 30 days to height 3,532,124 (3,737 of 6,352) are attributable to mining pools shielding transparent coinbase rewards into Sapling: 2,705 deposits carrying 31,228 ZEC, and at least 1,032 withdrawals carrying 16,432 ZEC that return those funds to transparent addresses. Most of these pools send the funds back to their own coinbase payout address shortly afterwards (F2Pool, Luxor, Kryptex, Mining Dutch), or on to a transparent payout transaction (2Miners), so the shielding is a round trip rather than a shielded payout to miners. ViaBTC and ViaBTC-Solo deposited a further 14,633 ZEC whose withdrawals could not be attributed. Together, pools that shield their coinbase into Sapling mined about 72% of blocks in that window.

Analysis of all 34,560 Mainnet blocks at heights 3,497,565 to 3,532,124 (2026-09-27 to 2026-10-27), using per-transaction data from the
. Transactions were classified by the sign of

: deposits (negative), withdrawals (positive beyond the fee, or with transparent or other shielded outputs), and internal transfers (otherwise). A deposit is attributed to a mining pool or to the ZCG funding stream when that party’s coinbase payout address supplied most of its transparent input value. A withdrawal is attributed to a pool when it pays that pool’s coinbase payout address, or when the value leaving Sapling exactly equals the sum of up to its number of Sapling spends of that pool’s deposits made in the preceding 4,032 blocks. Pool names are from CipherScan’s labels for the coinbase payout address. Hashpower share is estimated by share of blocks mined. Each block is assigned to the
if its coinbase transaction has Ironwood outputs; otherwise to the pool into which most of the in-window coinbase value of its miner payout address (excluding the funding stream address
) was subsequently shielded. This gives Sapling 71.6% of blocks and Ironwood 28.4% (23.8% by later sweep and 4.6% by shielded coinbase).
